title: Cardiac rhythm and sinus arrhythmia
why_this_matters: An irregular rhythm that would alarm a human clinician is normal in a resting dog, and a monitor read by human habit will misfire.

what_changes_from_human.point: Respiratory sinus arrhythmia is large and normal in a resting dog, more than three times the human amplitude in one study.
It is less marked at higher heart rates and absent during panting.

takeaway: Respiratory sinus arrhythmia is normal in a resting dog; read rhythm in context and hand off what you saw.

sources.citation: Grosso G et al. 2021. Breath-by-breath analysis of respiratory sinus arrhythmia in dogs. Respir Physiol Neurobiol.
Baisan RA et al. 2024. Quantification of respiratory sinus arrhythmia in control dogs and in dogs with various severity classes of myxomatous mitral valve disease. J Vet Cardiol.
Moise NS et al. 2020. Beat-to-beat patterning of sinus rhythm reveals non-linear rhythm in the dog compared to the human. Front Physiol.
Hanton G et al. 2006. The electrocardiogram of the Beagle dog: reference values and effect of sex, genetic strain, body position and heart rate. Lab Anim.

compare.human: Adult sinus rhythm is regular, with small respiratory variation.
compare.canine: Dogs have a clear respiratory sinus arrhythmia at rest. It averaged 40.1% of mean heart rate (peak to trough) in one study, more than three times the human value, and explained less than half of the canine sinus arrhythmia. Dog and human beat-to-beat patterns differ: the dog shows non-linear, wider interval distributions.
compare.implication: A variable heart rate that follows breathing is expected in a resting dog. Do not read it as abnormal on its own.

compare.topic: Effect of heart rate and panting
compare.canine: Sinus arrhythmia was less marked at high heart rates in a large Beagle ECG study but did not disappear. In two dogs, respiratory sinus arrhythmia was absent during panting.
compare.implication: A tachycardic or panting dog may show a regular-looking rhythm. Regularity is not proof of a normal dog.

compare.canine: In dogs with myxomatous mitral valve disease, loss of respiratory sinus arrhythmia is described as a negative prognostic factor, and the percentage decreased with disease severity up to acute congestive heart failure.
compare.implication: Absence of sinus arrhythmia in a calm resting dog is a finding worth reporting to the veterinarian.
